content.stem: A length is reported as 2.40 m and is multiplied by the exact number 3. What is the product to the same number of significant figures as the measured length?
content.solution: The exact multiplier does not limit precision. 2.40 has three significant figures, so 2.40 × 3 = 7.20 m.

content.stem: In the relation F = kv², F is force and v is speed. What are the SI base units of k?
content.solution: [k] = [F]/[v²] = (kg·m/s²)/(m²/s²) = kg/m.

content.stem: A walker moves 5 m east and then 5 m west in a total of 4 s. What is the average velocity?
content.solution: The final position equals the initial position. Average velocity is displacement divided by time, so it is 0/4 = 0 m/s.

content.stem: A particle's position in metres is x(t) = 2 + 3t + t², with t in seconds. What is its instantaneous velocity at t = 2 s?
content.solution: Velocity is dx/dt = 3 + 2t. At t = 2 s it is 7 m/s.

content.stem: A particle moves with constant acceleration along a line. Its displacement from x = 0 is 4 m at t = 1 s and 18 m at t = 3 s. What is its acceleration?
content.solution: Write s = ut + at²/2. At 1 s, u + a/2 = 4; at 3 s, 3u + 9a/2 = 18. Subtracting three times the first equation gives 3a = 6, hence a = 2 m/s².

content.stem: A displacement has perpendicular components 3 m east and 4 m north. What is its magnitude?
content.solution: The components form a right triangle, so the magnitude is √(3² + 4²) = 5 m.

content.stem: A projectile is launched from level ground with horizontal velocity component 10 m/s and initial upward component 20 m/s. It lands at the same height. With g = 10 m/s² and no air resistance, what is its horizontal range?
content.solution: Flight time is 2u_y/g = 2(20)/10 = 4 s. Horizontal speed stays 10 m/s, giving range 10 × 4 = 40 m.

content.stem: A projectile is launched at angle θ above level ground and lands at its launch height. Its horizontal range is four times its maximum height. With no air resistance and 0° < θ < 90°, what is θ?
content.solution: R = u²sin(2θ)/g and H = u²sin²θ/(2g), so R/H = 4cotθ. Since R/H = 4, cotθ = 1 and θ = 45° in the stated range.

content.stem: A 2 kg object has a net force of 6 N acting on it. What is the magnitude of its acceleration?
content.solution: Newton's second law gives a = F/m = 6/2 = 3 m/s².

content.stem: A 0.20 kg ball moving at 10 m/s along +x rebounds at 5 m/s along −x. What is the magnitude of the impulse on it?
content.solution: Impulse equals change in momentum: 0.20(−5 − 10) = −3 N·s. Its magnitude is 3 N·s.

content.stem: A constant 5 N force acts in the direction of a 4 m displacement. How much work does it do?
content.solution: Work is Fs cos 0° = 5 × 4 = 20 J.

content.stem: A 1 kg cart moving at 6 m/s collides with a stationary 2 kg cart. They stick together on a frictionless track. How much kinetic energy is lost in the collision?
content.solution: Momentum conservation gives final speed (1 × 6)/(1 + 2) = 2 m/s. Initial kinetic energy is 18 J; final energy is (3)(2²)/2 = 6 J. The loss is 12 J.

content.stem: A uniform solid disk of mass 2 kg and radius 0.50 m rotates about its central perpendicular axis. A constant net torque of 1 N·m acts on it. What is its angular acceleration?
content.solution: For this disk I = MR²/2 = 2(0.50)²/2 = 0.25 kg·m². Thus α = τ/I = 1/0.25 = 4 rad/s².

content.stem: Ignoring Earth's rotation, how does gravitational acceleration at distance 2R from Earth's centre compare with its value at radius R?

options.A: It is one quarter as large
options.D: It is four times as large

content.solution: Outside Earth, g = GM/r². Doubling r changes g by a factor of 1/2² = 1/4.

content.stem: For a circular orbit of radius R around a planet, speed is v. What is the circular-orbit speed around the same planet at radius 4R, neglecting all other bodies?
content.solution: Circular-orbit speed is √(GM/r). Replacing r by 4R gives v/2.

content.stem: A 100 N tensile force acts uniformly over a wire cross-sectional area of 2 × 10⁻⁴ m². What is the tensile stress?
content.solution: Stress is force per area: 100/(2 × 10⁻⁴) = 5 × 10⁵ Pa.

content.stem: A wire is 2 m long and has cross-sectional area 1 × 10⁻⁶ m² and Young's modulus 2 × 10¹¹ Pa. Within its elastic limit, how much does it extend under a 100 N tensile force?
content.solution: From Y = FL/(AΔL), extension ΔL = FL/(AY) = 100 × 2/(10⁻⁶ × 2 × 10¹¹) = 10⁻³ m = 1 mm.

content.stem: An ideal hydraulic lift has small and large piston areas in the ratio 1:10. A 20 N force acts on the small piston. What force does the fluid exert on the large piston?
content.solution: Pascal's law gives F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂. Therefore F₂ = 20 × 10 = 200 N.

content.stem: Water of density 1000 kg/m³ flows steadily through a horizontal ideal pipe. Its speed rises from 2 m/s at point 1 to 4 m/s at point 2. What is P₁ − P₂?
content.solution: At equal heights, Bernoulli's equation gives P₁ − P₂ = ρ(v₂² − v₁²)/2 = 1000(16 − 4)/2 = 6000 Pa.

content.stem: How much heat raises the temperature of 0.50 kg of a material by 10 K if its specific heat capacity is 400 J/(kg·K), with no phase change or heat loss?
A 2 m rod has linear expansion coefficient 1 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹. Its temperature rises by 50 K. What is its approximate increase in length?
A gas receives 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?
content.solution: With work done by the gas positive, the first law gives ΔU = Q − W = 500 − 200 = 300 J.

content.stem: A gas completes a rectangular p–V cycle. It expands from 1 × 10⁻³ m³ to 4 × 10⁻³ m³ at 3 × 10⁵ Pa, then returns to the starting volume at 1 × 10⁵ Pa. The other two legs are at constant volume. What is its net work done in one cycle?
content.solution: Only the constant-pressure legs do work. Net work is (3 × 10⁵ − 1 × 10⁵)(4 × 10⁻³ − 1 × 10⁻³) = 600 J, positive because expansion occurs at higher pressure.

content.stem: For the same ideal gas, absolute temperature rises from T to 4T. By what factor does its root-mean-square molecular speed change?
content.solution: At fixed molecular mass, v_rms = √(3k_BT/m), so multiplying T by 4 multiplies speed by √4 = 2.

content.stem: An ideal gas stays at constant pressure while its absolute temperature doubles. What happens to its mean-square molecular speed and its molecular number density, respectively?

options.A: Mean-square speed doubles; number density doubles
options.B: Mean-square speed doubles; number density halves
options.C: Mean-square speed halves; number density doubles
options.D: Mean-square speed and number density stay the same

content.solution: Kinetic theory gives mean-square speed proportional to T, so it doubles. Since P = nk_BT stays fixed while T doubles, number density n halves.

content.stem: For an ideal mass–spring oscillator, the mass is increased from m to 4m while the spring constant stays fixed. By what factor does the period change?
content.solution: T = 2π√(m/k), so replacing m by 4m multiplies T by √4 = 2.

content.stem: In ideal simple harmonic motion of amplitude A, what fraction of total mechanical energy is kinetic when displacement magnitude is A/2?
content.solution: Potential energy fraction is x²/A² = 1/4. With constant total energy, the kinetic fraction is 1 − 1/4 = 3/4.

content.stem: A progressive wave has frequency 240 Hz and wavelength 1.5 m. What is its speed?
content.solution: Wave speed v = fλ = 240 × 1.5 = 360 m/s.

content.stem: A string fixed at both ends is 0.75 m long. Transverse waves travel along it at 300 m/s. What is its third-harmonic frequency?
content.solution: The fundamental is v/(2L) = 300/(1.5) = 200 Hz. The third harmonic is 3 × 200 = 600 Hz.
